book.title: Difficult Conversations: How to Discuss What Matters Most
book.author: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton, Sheila Heen

chapterBreakdown.gentle: When something goes wrong in a relationship, most of us want to know whose fault it is. Blame feels like it makes sense: someone did something wrong, they should own it, and then things can move forward. But blame almost never moves things forward. It asks the wrong question. The question it asks — who deserves punishment — has an answer sometimes, but the answer does not change anything. The situation stays the same. What changes the situation is a different question: what is each of us doing that keeps this going, and what could each of us do differently? This is contribution. It is not about pretending everyone is equally responsible — contributions are almost never equal. It is about asking what each person can actually change. You cannot change what the other person did. You can change what you are doing. When you can see your own role in a pattern — even a small role — you have something to work with.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Blame focuses on who deserves punishment. Contribution focuses on what each person can change. These are different questions that point toward different actions. Blame is retrospective — it looks backward at who was wrong. Contribution is prospective — it looks at what each person is doing right now that keeps the situation going. Most difficult conversations are stuck not because blame is inaccurate but because blame cannot move anything. Naming what you contributed — even a small part — gives you something you can change. The other person's contribution is not in your direct control; yours is.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Blame is accurate and useless at the same time. It correctly identifies who did something wrong. It does nothing to change the situation, because it asks who deserves punishment rather than what can change next. Contribution asks the latter question. It identifies what each person is doing that keeps the pattern going. It does not claim everyone contributed equally — contributions are rarely equal. It locates what you can actually control: your own moves in the system. That is the lever you have access to. The other person's 90% is not yours to manage. Your 10% is.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
When a relationship goes wrong, the question most people ask first is: who is at fault? Blame has real appeal. It feels like clarity. Someone did something wrong, and naming it feels like the first step toward resolution. The problem is not that blame is usually wrong — it is often accurate. The problem is that blame asks a question that does not point toward change. Who deserves punishment? That question has an answer sometimes, but the answer does not move the situation forward. It moves it sideways. The blamed person gets defensive. The blamer feels unheard. Both people are now arguing about the past instead of thinking about what comes next.

Contribution asks a different question: what is each person doing right now that keeps this going, and what would it take for each to do something different? Contribution is not blame with softer language. It is a different temporal orientation. Blame looks backward; contribution looks at the present and future. Contribution is also not about pretending everyone contributed equally — contributions are almost never equal. Most situations break down more like 70/30 or 90/10. Contribution does not require claiming false parity. What it does is ask what each person can actually change.

The contribution system is the key concept here. Both people in a difficult conversation are usually playing roles in a pattern that keeps producing the same outcome. Each person's behavior triggers the other person's behavior, which triggers more of the first person's behavior. The pattern is self-reinforcing. Neither person is the cause and neither is the effect — they are both part of a system. The system, not the villain, is the target of change.

There are four recognizable patterns in how people contribute to difficult conversations. The first is avoiding until now: not raising an issue when it is small, so the delay becomes part of the problem. The second is being unapproachable: making it hard for the other person to raise something through defensiveness, volatility, or consistent dismissal. The third is style intersections: two people whose work styles or relational preferences are not wrong individually but produce friction when combined. The fourth is role assumptions: both people playing fixed roles in an interaction that guarantee the same result every time — the critic and the defender, the helper and the helpless, the pursuer and the avoider.

The hardest part of contribution-mapping is naming your own piece when the proportions are not equal. If you contributed 10% and the other person contributed 90%, naming your 10% can feel like it reduces their 90% or lets them off the hook. It does neither. Your 10% and their 90% are both real. Naming yours is not a claim that the proportions are equal — it is identifying the part of the system that is in your direct control. Their 90% is not. Yours is.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Blame and contribution ask different questions. Blame asks who deserves punishment — a backward-looking question that produces defensiveness and rarely changes anything. Contribution asks what each person is doing right now that keeps the situation going and what each could do differently — a forward-looking question that identifies actionable moves.

The contribution system: both people in a difficult conversation are usually playing roles in a pattern that keeps producing the same outcome. Each person's behavior triggers the other's, which reinforces the first person's behavior. The pattern is self-reinforcing. The system, not any individual, is what needs to change.

Four common contribution types. Avoiding until now: not raising an issue when it is small produces a delay that becomes part of the problem. Being unapproachable: defensiveness, volatility, or consistent dismissal makes it hard for the other person to bring something up. Style intersections: work styles or relational preferences that are not wrong individually but produce friction in combination. Role assumptions: both people have settled into fixed roles in their interaction that guarantee the same result — the organizer and the disengaged, the critic and the defender.

The asymmetric case: contributions are almost never equal. Naming your contribution does not require claiming the proportions are equal. If you contributed 10% and the other person contributed 90%, both are real and both can be named simultaneously. Naming your 10% is identifying what you can change. The other person's 90% is not in your direct control.

moreDetails.gentle: The avoiding-until-now contribution is one of the most common and least acknowledged. When you have not raised an issue for months and finally raise it, the delay itself is part of what has to be named — not as blame, but as context for how the situation calcified.

moreDetails.gentle: Most people resist naming their contribution in a highly unequal situation because it feels like it makes the other person's larger contribution seem smaller. It does not — both are real and both can be named. You are not claiming equality. You are claiming your own role.
moreDetails.direct: The reason to name your 10%: it is the only part of the system you have direct control over. The other person's behavior cannot be changed by your analysis of it — it can only be changed by them. Your behavior can be changed by your analysis of it.

point.gentle: Naming your contribution to a problem is not the same as forgiving the other person or accepting that what they did was okay. Both things can be true: you contributed to this AND the other person's contribution was larger AND their behavior was not acceptable.

point.competitive: The contribution frame keeps three things separate: what you did, what they did, and whether either was acceptable. These are independent variables. Naming your contribution is not taking a position on the other two.

Contribution-mapping is not universally safe — it has asymmetric risks depending on who is applying it and in what context.
moreDetails.competitive: In high-stakes or high-power-gap situations, contribution-mapping requires care. It is a tool for seeing the system, not a mechanism for equalizing responsibility. Its misuse — applying it to deflect accountability from a more powerful party — is a real failure mode.

activationPrompt.gentle: Think of a situation you have been framing as blame — where someone is clearly at fault. Can you name one specific thing you did that contributed to how the situation developed, even if your contribution was much smaller? What would it mean to name that?
activationPrompt.direct: Identify a stuck situation in your life. What contribution type does each party's role fall into: avoiding-until-now, unapproachability, style intersection, or role assumption? What is the contribution you have been least willing to name?
activationPrompt.competitive: Map a recurring difficult situation as a system. What is each party doing that triggers the other's behavior? Where is your 10% — the piece you can change? What would the system look like if you changed it?

selfCheckPrompt.gentle: In the situation you identified, if you named your contribution to the other person, would it change anything? What would you need to hold in mind to name it without claiming it equalizes the responsibility?
selfCheckPrompt.direct: Is there a situation where naming your contribution has felt like betraying yourself or making the other person's larger contribution disappear? What would it mean to hold both truths: I contributed, and their contribution was larger?
selfCheckPrompt.competitive: Identify the hardest contribution to name in a situation where the blame framing has felt accurate. What is the cost of naming it? What is the cost of not naming it?

oneMinuteRecap.connect: This connects to the intent/impact disentangle from the previous chapter. Just as acknowledging impact is not the same as accepting blame for intent, naming contribution is not the same as claiming equal responsibility.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Blame is not wrong. In most situations where we reach for it, it is accurate. The person who is being blamed did something that caused harm, and naming that is not a mistake. The problem with blame is not its accuracy — it is its uselessness for what comes next. Blame asks who deserves punishment. That is a backward-looking question, and it produces a specific backward-looking outcome: defensiveness in the blamed person, vindication in the blamer, and no change in the situation. The conversation goes sideways rather than forward.

Contribution asks a different question: what is each person doing right now that keeps this going, and what would each person need to do differently to produce a different outcome? Contribution is not blame with gentler language. It is a different temporal orientation. Blame establishes fault; contribution maps change. And contribution does not require pretending everyone contributed equally — contributions are almost never equal. In most situations the split is more like 70/30 or 90/10. The contribution framing does not claim otherwise. It identifies what each party can actually change, regardless of proportion.

The contribution system is where this becomes most useful. Both people in a difficult conversation are usually playing roles in a self-reinforcing pattern. Each person's behavior triggers the other's behavior, which reinforces the first person's behavior. The pattern runs on its own momentum. Neither person necessarily chose to start it, and neither can see their own role in it from inside the pattern. The system, not the villain, is what needs to change.

There are four recognizable contribution types. Avoiding until now: not raising an issue when it was small, so that the delay itself becomes part of the problem. Being unapproachable: creating conditions through defensiveness, volatility, or consistent dismissal that make it hard for the other person to raise something. The unapproachable person rarely knows they are unapproachable — their behavior produces avoidance in others, and what they see is people not raising things with them, which confirms their view that nothing is wrong. Style intersections: two people with work styles or relational preferences that produce friction in combination without either style being wrong individually. The friction is in the intersection, not in the parts. Role assumptions: both people have settled into fixed roles in their interaction — the organizer and the disengaged, the critic and the defender, the expert and the student — that guarantee the same result every time.

The hardest version of this chapter's move is naming your own contribution in a situation where your proportion is small and the other person's is large. This can feel like reducing their accountability — as if naming your 10% somehow diminishes their 90%. It does not. Both claims are real and independent. Your 10% is: you contributed to this outcome in a specific way. Their 90% is: their contribution was much larger, and that matters too. Naming yours is not a claim about the proportion — it is identifying the part of the system that is in your direct control. The other person's 90% is not yours to manage. Yours is.

The power-gap complication is the limit of this chapter's move that most treatments ignore. Contribution-mapping is not universally safe. In situations where the power differential is significant — a manager and a direct report, a senior colleague and a junior one, an institution and an individual — asking the less-powerful party to identify their contribution can become a mechanism for deflecting accountability from the more powerful party. A manager who uses contribution language with someone who raised a legitimate concern may be using the framework to avoid their own accountability. The contribution framing is a tool for seeing the system — it is not a mandate for symmetric responsibility in asymmetric situations.

moreDetails.competitive: The strategic reason to address feelings after contribution analysis: guilt and shame redirect into defensive behavior if they are not addressed. The person who has seen their own contribution and has not processed the feelings about it often becomes more defensive, not less, in the next conversation.

activationPrompt.gentle: Think of a situation you have been framing in terms of who is at fault. Without changing your assessment of who contributed more, can you name one specific thing you contributed to how the situation developed? What does naming it make available?
activationPrompt.direct: Identify a stuck situation. Map both parties' contributions using the four types. What is the system maintaining the pattern? What is your specific contribution to that system, and what would you need to change for the system to produce a different outcome?
activationPrompt.competitive: In a stuck situation where the blame framing has felt accurate, what is your 10%? If you named it and changed it, what would the system's dynamic have to look like in response? What is the cost of not naming it?

prompt.gentle: In the situation you have been thinking about, is there a contribution type that applies to you? Avoiding-until-now? Being hard to approach? A style that produces friction in the combination? A role you have been playing? What would it mean to name it?
prompt.direct: Identify a situation where naming your contribution has felt like it would reduce the other party's accountability. Hold both claims simultaneously: I contributed AND their contribution was much larger. What makes this hard? What makes it important?
prompt.competitive: In a high-stakes situation, trace the contribution system. Which party is more powerful? Is contribution-mapping being applied symmetrically? If the less-powerful party is being asked to name their contribution before the more powerful party's behavior is addressed, what is happening to the framework?

prompt.gentle: Is there a situation where you have been playing a role — organizer, critic, helper, defender — for so long that the role no longer feels like a choice? What would it look like to step out of the role, and what would the other person's role become if you did?
prompt.direct: Trace a recurring pattern. What is the self-reinforcing loop? What does each party do that triggers the other's behavior? Where is the intervention point — the move that, if changed, would disrupt the system rather than just repeat it?
prompt.competitive: Identify your most invisible contribution type in a specific situation. The avoiding-until-now you have not acknowledged, the unapproachability you cannot see from inside, the style intersection you have attributed to the other party. What would become possible if you named it?

predictionPrompt.gentle: If you named your contribution to a situation where your proportion was small — not to claim it was equal, but just to name it — what do you predict the other person would be able to hear that they could not hear before?
predictionPrompt.direct: If Dara sends the message to Felix — 'I've been less communicative than usual, and I think that's made things harder for both of us' — without claiming Felix's oversight was acceptable, what do you predict happens to the system?
predictionPrompt.competitive: In a situation where the power gap is significant, what do you predict happens if contribution-mapping is applied symmetrically (both parties name their contribution) versus asymmetrically (only the less-powerful party is asked)?

oneMinuteRecap.retrieve: Blame is retrospective; contribution is prospective. Both parties in a difficult conversation are usually in a contribution system. Four contribution types: avoiding-until-now, unapproachability, style intersections, role assumptions. Contributions are rarely equal. Naming yours identifies what you can change.
oneMinuteRecap.connect: This extends the intent/impact disentangle from the previous chapter. Just as 'I caused harm' and 'I intended harm' are independent claims, 'I contributed' and 'their contribution was larger' are independent claims. Naming yours does not erase theirs.
oneMinuteRecap.preview: Seeing your own contribution often surfaces feelings — guilt, grief, relief. Those feelings need somewhere to go before they can be useful. The next chapter is about what to do with feelings in a difficult conversation.

scenario.gentle: Dara, a remote employee, has been going quiet for three months — submitting work without comment, not responding in the team channel, declining optional meetings. Her manager Felix has responded by adding check-ins, asking more questions, and adding her to Slack threads she doesn't need to be on. Dara experiences Felix's behavior as controlling; Felix experiences Dara's silence as a performance concern. Dara is now drafting a message to HR. The question: does she send the HR message, or does she look at the contribution system first?
scenario.direct: Three-month cycle: Dara withdraws, Felix increases oversight, Dara withdraws further. Both are right about what the other is doing and blind to their own contribution. Dara is drafting a message to HR. Should she, or should she try to map the system first?
scenario.competitive: Dara's withdrawal triggered Felix's oversight. Felix's oversight triggered more withdrawal. Self-reinforcing cycle, three months in. Dara is at a decision point: HR complaint or contribution analysis?

whatToDo.gentle: Dara names her contribution: she has been less communicative than usual, and that has made the situation harder for both of them. She sends Felix a message: 'I've been less communicative than usual, and I think that's made things harder for both of us. Can we talk?' Not a concession — her assessment of Felix's oversight as excessive does not change. But it names her contribution to the system and opens a different kind of conversation.
whatToDo.direct: Dara identifies her contribution (withdrawal created the information gap that Felix's oversight is filling) and sends a message naming it without claiming Felix's oversight is appropriate. 'I've been less communicative than usual. Can we talk?' This names her lever — the thing she can actually change.
whatToDo.competitive: Dara's lever: her own communication. She sends a message naming her withdrawal as a contribution without claiming it excuses Felix's behavior. This shifts the system rather than escalating it to HR.

whyItMatters.gentle: If Dara sends the HR message without naming her contribution to the system, the system continues. The oversight will be noted, perhaps adjusted, but the underlying dynamic — Dara's withdrawal as the condition that produces the oversight — will not change. Naming her contribution opens a different conversation: one about the pattern, not just the behavior.
whyItMatters.direct: The HR escalation targets Felix's behavior but not the system. The system will route around a one-sided intervention. Naming Dara's contribution targets the system directly — both parties' roles are on the table, and change becomes possible.
whyItMatters.competitive: The HR move is single-party targeting. It may reduce Felix's oversight in the short term and will not change the underlying dynamic. The contribution move changes the conditions for the other party's behavior by changing one's own.

scenario.gentle: A group project just ended. In the postmortem, the group's consensus is that Nola under-contributed. She missed two meetings, delivered her section late, and produced less than the others. The group is frustrated and the analysis stays focused on Nola. No one asks what the group dynamics were that made it easy for Nola to drift. No one names their own role in how the pattern developed.
scenario.direct: Group project postmortem. The group diagnoses Nola as the free-rider. This is accurate. The group also does not examine: who could have raised the pattern earlier and didn't, whose communication style made Nola harder to reach, how the group's roles set up a dynamic where Nola's low contribution was enabled.
scenario.competitive: The postmortem targets Nola as the free-rider. Accurate. It also misses the contribution system: how did the group's dynamics make it easy for the pattern to persist? What contribution types are invisible in this room?

whatToDo.gentle: A more complete postmortem asks not just who under-contributed but what the group did — or did not do — that made the under-contribution possible. Did anyone raise the concern early, when it would have been easier to address? Did Nola's quietness get noticed and named? Were roles clear enough that under-contribution became visible before the deadline?
whatToDo.direct: The group names Nola's contribution and then asks about the system: What did each of us contribute to how this developed? Who avoided raising the concern? Was anyone unapproachable? What about the group's structure made Nola's drift easy to miss?
whatToDo.competitive: The complete contribution analysis: Nola's free-riding is one piece of the system. The group's avoiding-until-now (not raising it earlier), role ambiguity (no one clearly responsible for tracking progress), and unapproachability (one member who shut down concerns early) are the other pieces. Map all of them.

whyItMatters.gentle: A postmortem that only names Nola's contribution will produce the same result next time, with a different Nola. The pattern is the structure that enables free-riding; that structure is what the group can actually change. Naming it is the only postmortem that prevents recurrence.
whyItMatters.direct: The hidden cost: a postmortem that misses the group's contribution to the system will repeat the pattern in the next project. The group has accurate information about Nola's behavior and incomplete information about the conditions that allowed it. The incomplete information is what they will bring to the next project.
whyItMatters.competitive: The group analysis that stops at Nola has incomplete information. The contribution system analysis has complete information. Complete information produces better calibration for the next project.

scenario.gentle: Marta and Sione are having their annual holiday conversation, which always starts as a logistics discussion and always ends with both people frustrated. Marta raises that she handles everything; Sione defends the arrangement. This year, something is different: Marta names her contribution before naming her complaint.
scenario.direct: Marta and Sione's tenth version of the holiday conversation. Marta opens by naming her contribution to the pattern: her competence at logistics has made it unnecessary for Sione to develop any logistics capacity. Sione can hear this in a way he could not hear 'you never help.'
scenario.competitive: Marta shifts from blame framing ('you never help') to contribution framing ('my competence has enabled your disengagement'). This is a different conversation with different room for change.

whatToDo.gentle: Marta says: 'I've been so good at handling all of this that I've made it unnecessary for you to ever care about it. That's part of why we're here.' This is different from 'you never help.' It names the system. Sione can hear his own contribution differently when the conversation is not about his failure but about a pattern both people have maintained.
whatToDo.direct: Marta names her contribution (competence-enabling-disengagement) before naming her complaint. Sione names his (conflict-avoidance-enabling-burden). Both contributions are in the room. The conversation is now about the system rather than Sione's fault.
whatToDo.competitive: Contribution-framing this conversation: Marta's contribution named explicitly, Sione's named explicitly, both people looking at the pattern together. This is a different kind of conversation than the one they have had ten times.

whyItMatters.gentle: The conversation Marta has been having for ten years does not change because blame is inaccurate — it doesn't change because blame cannot address the system. Naming contributions opens the conversation to the system, and the system is what can actually change.
whyItMatters.direct: The relationship turn: when Marta names her contribution, Sione can hear his without defending against an accusation. The conversation becomes about the pattern rather than about Sione's failure. That is a conversation both people can have.
whyItMatters.competitive: The blame conversation has been running for ten years without producing change. The contribution conversation is running for the first time. The difference is not the topic — it is the question each framing asks and what kind of response it makes possible.

scenario.gentle: Yemi is planning to raise a concern with Kwame about the delivery timeline. Yemi's view: Kwame takes too long. Kwame delivers late every quarter. Yemi has the data. Question: if Yemi raises the concern from the blame frame — 'you're consistently late' — will it change anything?
scenario.direct: Yemi is about to raise the timeline concern with Kwame using blame framing: 'You're consistently late.' Kwame's view: Yemi's work is rough when delivered and requires significant revision, which is why Kwame takes time. Neither has told the other. Prediction: does blame framing produce change?
scenario.competitive: Yemi's complaint is accurate. Kwame is late. Prediction: does an accurate blame complaint change Kwame's behavior? What would contribution framing reveal?

whatToDo.gentle: Reveal: Kwame's lateness is produced partly by the rough state of Yemi's deliverables, which require significant revision before Kwame can build on them. Yemi's complaint is accurate and does not capture the style intersection producing the timeline. Contribution framing: 'I deliver early and rough; you deliver late and comprehensive. We have been working from incompatible definitions of done.' That conversation can produce change.
whatToDo.direct: Reveal: the accurate blame complaint produces defensiveness in Kwame and does not change the pattern, because the pattern is a style intersection, not just Kwame's failure. Contribution framing locates the intersection and makes both parties' contributions visible.
whatToDo.competitive: Reveal: accurate blame, predictable defense, no system change. Contribution framing: maps the intersection, makes both parties' contributions visible, opens negotiation about expectations. Different outcomes.

whyItMatters.gentle: The blame complaint might produce a short-term adjustment in Kwame's behavior. It will not produce a change in the underlying style intersection, because the blame complaint does not name the intersection. Contribution framing names what actually needs to change.
whyItMatters.direct: The broader principle: blame that is accurate but incomplete misses the system. The complaint about Kwame's lateness is accurate and misses the contribution on Yemi's side that produces the pattern. Complete information about the system produces different interventions.
whyItMatters.competitive: Accurate blame on one side of a style intersection does not produce system change. Both sides of the intersection have to be mapped for change to be possible.

scenario.gentle: Isabel wants to raise a concern with her project group that the group leader, Sage, contributed to the project's poor performance by being dismissive of alternative approaches early on. Isabel's hesitation: she is worried that naming Sage's contribution will come across as blame. How does she raise Sage's contribution without it landing as an accusation?
scenario.direct: Isabel needs to name Sage's contribution to the group's poor outcome. She is worried it will land as blame. What is the framing that keeps it in contribution language rather than blame language?
scenario.competitive: Isabel has an accurate contribution analysis: Sage's early dismissiveness closed off approaches that might have worked. She needs to name it without triggering a defensive response that closes the conversation. What is the framing?

whatToDo.gentle: The contribution framing: 'I think the early dismissal of some of the alternative approaches made it harder for the group to find a different direction when the original plan ran into trouble. I want to name that as part of what produced our outcome.' This names the contribution as a contribution to a system — not as a character judgment about Sage.
whatToDo.direct: Isabel names the behavior's contribution to the outcome without attributing intent or character: 'When alternative approaches got closed off early, the group lost flexibility. That is part of what produced the result.' Contribution framing, not blame framing.
whatToDo.competitive: Isabel's contribution frame: name what the behavior produced in the system, not what it says about Sage as a person. 'The early closures cost the group options' — this is a contribution analysis, not a blame verdict.

whyItMatters.gentle: The difference between blame and contribution framing in this context: blame says 'Sage failed the group.' Contribution says 'Sage's behavior produced a specific system effect.' The second framing makes the conversation about the pattern, which can change, rather than about Sage's character, which cannot.
whyItMatters.direct: The self-diagnosis: Isabel can practice distinguishing blame and contribution framing in her own preparation. If her language points toward Sage's character or fault, it is blame framing. If it points toward what Sage's behavior produced in the system, it is contribution framing.
whyItMatters.competitive: The framing distinction is the lever Isabel is practicing. Blame triggers defense and closes the postmortem. Contribution maps the system and opens the conversation about what the group can change next time.

scenario.gentle: Dani and her partner have a recurring argument about emotional connection. Dani's recurring complaint: 'You never initiate.' Before: Dani raises it as a blame complaint about her partner's behavior. After: she maps her own contribution to the pattern.
scenario.direct: Dani's blame framing: 'You never initiate.' Before and after: she names her contribution to the pattern (her life runs on schedules, including emotional ones, and her partner cannot connect on a schedule) and the conversation changes.
scenario.competitive: Blame framing: 'You never initiate.' Contribution framing: Dani has structured the relationship's emotional life around scheduled connection, and her partner cannot connect on demand. Both contributions are in the system.

whatToDo.gentle: After: Dani names her contribution. 'I have built our life together on scheduled things, and I think I have been expecting you to connect emotionally on a schedule too. That might not be how you work.' This does not make her complaint disappear — she still needs more initiation. But it names her contribution to the dynamic that has been making initiation harder.
whatToDo.direct: Dani names her contribution: the scheduling structure she has created has made spontaneous connection harder for both of them. 'I wonder if I have been asking you to connect emotionally the way I connect emotionally, and that might not be how you work.' This is a contribution analysis of her own role in the pattern.
whatToDo.competitive: Dani's contribution: the scheduled-life structure is her contribution to the conditions making initiation hard. Naming it changes what she can ask: not 'initiate more' but 'here is the system we are in — what would make connection feel more natural for you?'

whyItMatters.gentle: The before framing keeps the conversation focused on her partner's failure and does not locate what Dani could change. The after framing opens a conversation about the system both people have built, and what both could do differently.
whyItMatters.direct: The behavior shift: when Dani names her contribution to the pattern, she gains information she did not have before — about how her own behavior has shaped the conditions she is complaining about. This changes the question she can ask and the change she can request.
whyItMatters.competitive: The contribution analysis opens a negotiation that blame cannot. Blame produces defense. Contribution opens the possibility that both parties' moves are on the table and both can change.

reviewCards.title: Blame vs. Contribution
reviewCards.content: When a situation has gone wrong, can you identify the difference between asking 'who is at fault?' and asking 'what is each of us doing that keeps this going?' What does the second question make available that the first does not?

reviewCards.title: Mapping the Contribution System
reviewCards.content: In a stuck situation, can you identify what each party is doing that triggers the other party's behavior? Where is the self-reinforcing loop? What would each party need to change for the pattern to produce a different result?

reviewCards.title: Naming Your 10%
reviewCards.content: In a situation where your contribution is much smaller than the other person's, can you name your piece without claiming the proportions are equal? What is the specific thing you did that contributed to how the situation developed, regardless of how it compares to what the other person did?

reviewCards.title: The Four Contribution Types
reviewCards.content: Which of the four contribution types applies to your role in a current stuck situation: avoiding-until-now, being hard to approach, a style intersection, or a fixed role assumption? What makes that contribution hard to see from inside it?

reviewCards.title: When Contribution-Mapping Has Limits
reviewCards.content: Is there a situation where applying contribution-mapping to the less-powerful party before addressing the more powerful party's behavior would deflect accountability rather than map the system? What makes contribution-mapping a system-analysis tool rather than a responsibility-equalization tool?

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Blame asks who deserves punishment. That question looks backward and rarely changes anything. Contribution asks what each person is doing that keeps the situation going. Contributions are almost never equal — naming yours does not claim the proportions are equal. It names what you can actually change.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Blame is retrospective and produces defensiveness. Contribution is prospective and maps what each person can change. Both parties in a difficult conversation are usually in a contribution system — a self-reinforcing pattern both people are maintaining. Seeing the system, and your role in it, is what makes change possible.
keyTakeawayCard.competitive: Blame establishes fault. Contribution maps what each party can change. These are different moves with different information value. Contributions are almost never equal. Naming your 10% does not claim parity — it locates your only direct lever. The system changes when someone changes their move in it.
